$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(10 x^{2} + 5 x)=20 x + 5.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=25=25,
$$

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(25)}=- \frac{1}{25}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(15)&=- \frac{1}{25}(x-(1))\\y&=- \frac{1}{25}x-(- \frac{1}{25})+(15)\\y&=- \frac{1}{25}x+\frac{376}{25}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(6\sqrt{x^{3}})\\&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(6 x^{\frac{3}{2}})\\&=9x^{1/2}\\&=9 \sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=9=9,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(9)}=- \frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(6)&=- \frac{1}{9}(x-(1))\\y&=- \frac{1}{9}x-(- \frac{1}{9})+(6)\\y&=- \frac{1}{9}x+\frac{55}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}- \frac{1}{9}x+\frac{55}{9}&=0\\x&=55.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at  $(55,0).$

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3/2}) \\  & =3{x}^{1/2} \\  & =3\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=3\sqrt{1}=3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{1}{3}+2 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at  $(7,0).$

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=9\sqrt[3]{x^{2}}$ at the point $(8,36)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(9\sqrt[3]{x^{2}})\\&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(9 x^{\frac{2}{3}})\\&=6x^{-1/3}\\&=\frac{6}{\sqrt[3]{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(8)=3=3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(3)}=- \frac{1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(36)&=- \frac{1}{3}(x-(8))\\y&=- \frac{1}{3}x-(- \frac{8}{3})+(36)\\y&=- \frac{1}{3}x+\frac{116}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y&=- \frac{1}{3}\cdot0+\frac{116}{3}\\y&=\frac{116}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,\frac{116}{3}).$
